title: The illness
hook: he falls ill and is nursed in Aisha's room

segments.voice: Yesterday, akmaltu, this day I have perfected: the verse at Arafah that said the religion was whole. Your line was completed.

A glass of water on the side table. Curtains half drawn. Voices lowered in the hall. A sickroom has the same hush in every century. Back in Medina, not long after the farewell pilgrimage, the Prophet ﷺ began to suffer from a severe headache and fever. It didn't pass. He kept going to the mosque as long as he could, and kept to his custom of spending each night with one of his wives in turn. But he grew weaker, and he kept asking, the reports say: where am I tomorrow?
screen: `A SICKBED IN MEDINA.` → `HEADACHE AND FEVER.` → `WHERE AM I TOMORROW?`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari tells it through Aisha. When the illness grew heavy, he asked his wives for permission to be nursed in her room, and they all agreed. Even sick, he asked. He walked there leaning on two men, his feet dragging a line in the dirt. That small room, next to the mosque, is where his last days happened. Companions came in and out. His daughter Fatimah came. Aisha nursed him. And all his life he had been the visitor at other people's sickbeds. The reports show him there again and again, and once, al-Bukhari says, at the bedside of a Jewish boy who had served him and fallen ill; he invited the boy to Islam, and the boy accepted. He listed visiting the sick among the rights one Muslim has over another. The Arabic for this visiting is 'iyadah. A hadith qudsi, words he reported from God, preserved in Sahih Muslim, takes it further. On the Day of Judgment, God will say: son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me. The person says: how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds? And God says: my servant was sick and you did not visit him. Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him. It closes a week of hard lessons: numbers didn't help, the truth saved them, they came from everywhere, all in white, no one above another, completed. Now, the sickroom.
screen: `EVEN SICK, HE ASKED PERMISSION.` · `THE ROOM BESIDE THE MOSQUE.` · `HE HAD ALWAYS VISITED THE SICK.` · `YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.` · then, large: `VISIT THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Who's unwell in your life right now: someone in the hospital, someone whose illness has gone on so long people have stopped asking, someone recovering at home, someone struggling in their mind? Picture them and the room they're in, and choose how you'd reach them: a visit, a call, a message, a meal left at the door. If you pray, you can pray for their healing now.
The illness. The Prophet's last sickness, nursed in Aisha's room, and a reminder of how he always visited the sick. Today's word.
Your line: visit the sick. Five minutes of your voice may be the best part of their day. That's day two hundred eighty-seven.

screen: `DAY 287 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ABU BAKR LEADS THE PRAYER.`

howItsDone: Muslims count visiting the sick, 'iyadah, as a right owed between Muslims and a deed of great reward, and pray for the healing of the people they visit.

what a scholar hears: Aisha's account in al-Bukhari, and the hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim 2569 where God identifies with the sick: you would have found Me with him.

chat.says: What did the Prophet teach about visiting people who are sick?
options: It's one of the rights Muslims owe each other, and he did it all his life.
It's kind, but best left to family, so the sick can rest.
Only when the sick person asks you to come, never on your own.
chat.meaning: He listed visiting the sick among the rights Muslims owe one another, and visited the sick again and again, even a Jewish boy.

hadith qudsi.meaning: words the Prophet reported from God

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 198, 4442, 1356, 1240; Muslim 2569) cited from memory; confirm.
'Where am I tomorrow?' is from Aisha's report in al-Bukhari (4450) as remembered; confirm.
In the hadith of the Jewish boy, the boy accepts Islam before dying; the script mentions only the visit. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with that.
